fullName: X-ray Photon Correlation Spectroscopy beamline (8-ID-E wide-angle XPCS and 8-ID-I small-angle XPCS)

status2026.detail: Operational and accepting general users (APS directory, 2026). 8-ID was the first APS-U feature beamline to host users: the first post-upgrade user run began on 16 September 2024, the 8-ID home page dates General User Program operation from October 2024, and a University of Akron group is reported as the first users in early November 2024, while the beamline was in final commissioning (a small date discrepancy between sources). Operated by the XSD Dynamics & Structure group; 8-ID-E (wide-angle XPCS) and 8-ID-I (small-angle XPCS and Rheo-SAXS-XPCS) run one at a time. The GISAXS/GIWAXS program that used to share the old 8-ID-E has moved to 9-ID-D (CSSI), so 8-ID-E is now dedicated to WA-XPCS. The storage ring reached its 200 mA design current on 4 February 2025. Construction milestones: the old 8-ID-E/I enclosures were emptied in under 14 days (reported 3 October 2022); the XPCS SAXS detector positioner and WAXS goniometer appear on the experiment floor in the December 2023 installation-status slides.

tagline: Coherent X-rays make a grainy speckle pattern that twinkles as matter moves; timing the twinkle reveals motion from hopping atoms to drifting nanoparticles.
summary: 8-ID times how matter moves, from drifting nanoparticles down to shuffling atoms. Shine a laser pointer through water clouded with a drop of milk and the spot on the wall turns grainy and twinkles: the grain, called speckle, is an interference pattern set by where every fat droplet sits, and it changes as they jiggle. X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS) does the same with coherent X-rays, whose waves march in step and whose wavelength is about the size of an atom, so it can follow motion too small, too fast or too deeply buried for a light microscope. Cameras record up to 56,000 frames a second, and software measures how fast each pattern changes. Two stations take turns: 8-ID-E looks at wide angles for atomic-scale motion, 8-ID-I at small angles with a detector up to 12 m away. In late 2024, 8-ID became the first upgraded feature beamline to host users.

whatAPSUEnables.text: Speckle timing needs enough coherent photons, X-rays whose waves march in step, in each frame. Faster motion means shorter frames and fewer photons. In the design's brightness mode, the upgraded ring's electron beam has root-mean-square widths of about 15 × 4 µm instead of 275 × 10 µm, and at a given energy coherent flux grows in step with brightness: the design value at 20 keV rises roughly 250–500-fold. This opens up weak scatterers such as proteins and dilute particles, and coherent X-rays up to 25 keV that pass through rheometers, furnaces and pressure cells. When photon counts set the limit, the shortest usable frame time falls as one divided by coherent flux squared: a 100× gain can give 10,000× shorter frames. This holds at fixed acquisition time, speckle contrast and pixel count; at fixed frame time the signal-to-noise gain is only 100×. Detector speed and dose can limit the gain. These are design values; no published measurement of the as-built coherent flux had been found by October 2026.
quantitative: Coherent flux at 20 keV (undulator optimized for 20 keV): 0.6 × 10¹¹ ph/s for the 2019 APS → 312 × 10¹¹ ph/s in APS-U brightness mode or 148 × 10¹¹ ph/s in timing mode, a gain of ~250–500×.
Time resolution: 19.2 µs continuous and ~1 µs in burst mode (Rigaku 3-Mpixel detector); the design goal is 100 ns.

Electron beam at the insertion device: 280 × 10 µm rms (H × V) before the upgrade vs ~14.5 × 3.1 µm (flat beam, κ = 0.1) or 12.3 × 8.3 µm (round beam) at zero current. APS describes this as ~15 × 4 µm vs 275 × 10 µm, up to 500× brighter.
Measured APS-U horizontal emittance: 33 pm·rad at the full 200 mA (April 2025); below 30 pm·rad at reduced current with full coupling.
Design coherent flux in one transverse mode, Si(111), SA-XPCS: 1.7 × 10¹³ ph/s at 10 keV, 7.2 × 10¹² at 15 keV and 2.0 × 10¹² at 25 keV (κ = 0.1).
PDR world comparison, one 1 × 1 mode at 0.01% bandwidth: APS-U 6 × 10¹² ph/s at 12 keV and 9 × 10¹¹ at 20 keV, vs 8 × 10¹⁰ / 2 × 10¹⁰ at PETRA III P10 and 8 × 10¹⁰ / 5 × 10⁹ at NSLS-II CHX.

Pre-upgrade 8-ID-I benchmark: ~2 × 10¹⁰ ph/s at 7.4 keV through a 20 × 150 µm (H × V) coherence-defining slit, with a Ge(111) monochromator (~0.03% bandpass) and two 3.3 cm Undulator A devices; measured speckle contrast ~10%. That beam was only partially coherent (several horizontal modes), so it is not a strict one-mode value.

Directory flux: 10¹³ ph/s at 9 keV with Si(111) and 3 × 10¹² ph/s at 9 keV with Si(311); beam 6 × 3 µm focused, 20 × 20 µm unfocused. The directory does not say whether these are coherent or total flux.

Detector lineage at 8-ID-I before the upgrade: the UFXC32k prototype reached 826 ns burst frames and 19.36 µs continuous frames (2018); the Rigaku XSPA-500k ran at 52 kHz (20 µs) with up to ~10⁹ frames a day reduced in near real time (2021).
Original 2015 APS-U proposal goal: dynamics from 10 ns to 1,000 s and length scales from 1 nm to 5 µm, expanding the dynamic range of XPCS by up to six orders of magnitude.
Accessible time scales quoted for APS-U-era XPCS at the APS: 100 ns to 1,000 s; for WA-XPCS, 'gapless coverage from µs to hours'.
Data: up to ~20 PB of raw data a year vs ~0.1 PB a year at pre-upgrade 8-ID; the Rigaku 3M at 56 kHz produces ~164 GB/s raw.

Derived here (Gaussian beams, Kim convention, zero current, 10 keV, 4.7 m undulator): coherent fraction ~9% for the APS-U flat beam vs ~0.06% for the 2019 APS, about 160× (an estimate that ignores energy spread).

2021 WA-XPCS instrument table: coherent flux (one mode) 1–2 × 10¹² ph/s with Si(111) over 8–25 keV, about 10× below the FDR/PDR one-mode values at 8.8–10 keV. The cause (KB/CRL losses, different assumptions or a typo) is not documented.

Cross-check of the coherent fraction: the 2015 Early Science report describes the pre-upgrade APS beam near 11 keV as ~10,000 coherent modes, rising to a coherent fraction of order 10% with APS-U, consistent with the ~0.06% → ~9% estimate above.
APS Strategic Plan 2025–29: a '4-to-6-order-of-magnitude increase in the time resolution of XPCS'; accessible time scales 100 ns to 1,000 s.

techniques.name: Small-angle X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy
techniques.text: Small-angle XPCS follows how a speckle pattern at small scattering angles changes over time, to reveal how nanoparticles, polymers or proteins move over distances from about a nanometre to a micrometre. Each ring of the pattern belongs to one length scale, set by the scattering vector q (smaller angles mean larger distances), and the software measures how quickly the speckle at each q loses its resemblance to its earlier self, a curve called the intensity autocorrelation function g_{2}. For freely diffusing particles, that decay time shrinks as 1/q²; jammed or glassy materials often show ballistic motion (decay time ∝ 1/q) and faster-than-exponential decays, signs of internal stress relaxing. At 8-ID-I the coherent spot is 3–10 µm and the detector sits 4–12 m from the sample; one published run at 12.4 keV with the detector at 11.6 m covered q = 0.04–0.51 nm⁻¹.

techniques.name: Wide-angle X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (incl. Bragg/diffuse XPCS)
techniques.text: Wide-angle XPCS applies the same speckle timing at large scattering angles, where the speckle comes from the arrangement of atoms and crystal domains. It can catch atoms rearranging in a glass, or charge and magnetic patterns flickering in quantum materials. Atomic-scale speckle is fine, so 8-ID-E focuses the beam to 0.3–3 µm (a smaller spot makes larger speckle) and places the detector 1.5–4 m away, reaching scattering vectors up to about 4.7 Å⁻¹ at 10 keV with the long-distance positioner. At wide angles, X-rays scattered from different depths and from across the beam's width travel paths of different length, which washes out the speckle unless the energy spread is small. The Si(311) crystal setting, which passes a narrower band of energies, is often needed: its longitudinal coherence, the path difference over which the waves stay in step, is about 4.6 µm against 0.9 µm for Si(111) at 10 keV.

techniques.name: Rheo-XPCS (Rheo-SAXS-XPCS)
techniques.text: Rheo-XPCS puts a fluid in a rheometer, which shears or oscillates it, while speckle timing watches its nanoscale structure, linking what you feel when you stir (thickness, springiness) to what the particles are actually doing. The rheometer, offered with Argonne's Center for Nanoscale Materials, holds the sample in the gap between two concentric cylinders (a Couette cell); the beam crosses the cell along the direction in which the flow speed changes, so the speckle records motion both along the flow and along the cylinder axis. Stress, strain and recovery are measured at the same time as the speckle movies, and two-time and heterodyne analyses reveal mobile and arrested regions side by side, such as shear bands and jammed networks.

techniques.name: Pinhole ultra-small-angle scattering / US-XPCS
techniques.text: For the largest structures, the sample sits on the diffractometer in 8-ID-E and the detector at the far end of the 8-ID-I flight tube, about 22 m away. A longer distance spreads small angles over more pixels, so this pinhole ultra-small-angle X-ray scattering (USAXS) mode resolves angles well below those of the normal small-angle setup, reaching structures up to micrometres in size and their slow motion (US-XPCS). It uses a 15–45 µm beam, set in the 2021 functional requirements.

techniques.name: Two-time correlation and higher-order analysis
techniques.text: Instead of one averaged answer, two-time correlation compares every frame with every other frame. The result is a square map, C(t_{1}, t_{2}), with time running along both axes: distance from the diagonal is the delay between two frames, and position along it is the age of the sample. Its shape shows when a material speeds up, slows down as it ages, or moves in sudden avalanches, which a single time-averaged correlation curve would blur, so it is the tool of choice for aging glasses and for soft materials recovering after shear. At 8-ID the maps are computed on graphics processors in near real time with the boost-corr software and inspected in pyXPCSviewer; machine learning helps sort them, and higher-order and spatio-temporal correlations are still being developed.

techniques.name: Heterodyne XPCS / X-ray velocimetry
techniques.text: When some scatterers flow and others stay put, their speckle fields interfere and the intensity beats, like two slightly out-of-tune guitar strings; the beat frequency gives the flow speed. This mixing of a moving signal with a static reference is called heterodyning. In the correlation function it appears as an oscillation, cos(q·vτ), on top of the usual decay, where v is the velocity and q the scattering vector, so only the velocity component along q is measured. 8-ID uses it as a nanoscale velocity meter for flow, convection and shear-thickening networks, and a newer transport-coefficient analysis extracts flow directly from data far from equilibrium.

scienceCases.title: Why some fluids turn solid when punched: shear thickening seen from inside
scienceCases.text: Push slowly into a dense suspension, such as cornstarch in water, and it flows; punch it and it locks up. At 8-ID-I, speckle timing inside a rheometer (Rheo-XPCS) followed silica nanoparticles (200 and 360 nm, filling 56–60.5% of the volume) in polyethylene glycol as they were sheared towards this shear-thickening transition, and for at least an hour after the shear stopped. Beats in the speckle, where light scattered by moving particles mixed with light from stuck ones (heterodyning), showed mobile particles moving against a jammed, frictional network. The stress relaxed quickly, but the structure and dynamics took much longer. The data appear to pre-date the upgrade shutdown (the 'dark period'), an inference from publication timing.

scienceCases.title: Memory and relaxation in soft glasses after flow
scienceCases.text: Squish a soft glassy material and let go, and it partly springs back. A recent study at 8-ID that timed speckle inside a rheometer followed the nanoscale motion during this slow recovery after a 300% strain: the stress decayed almost logarithmically, in step with the loss of recoverable strain, while a convection-like backflow split the sample into bands that move differently. The run used 12.4 keV X-rays, an 8 × 8 µm spot and an EIGER2 X CdTe 4M detector 11.6 m from the sample. The preprint gives no run date; that the data are post-upgrade is inferred from that distance, beyond the ~10 m maximum of the old station.

scienceCases.title: Atoms that move in bursts: aging of a metallic glass
scienceCases.text: Metallic glasses are metals whose atoms are frozen in a jumble rather than a crystal. Wide-angle X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS) watched a zirconium-based bulk metallic glass held at 668 K, just below its glass transition, for 83 hours, one frame every 2.5 s. Instead of one smooth relaxation, periods of steady aging alternated with intermittent, burst-like rearrangements of atomic clusters, with the dynamics converging towards an anomalous form of diffusion that the ordinary (Fickian) law does not describe. The speckle was recorded at the main diffraction halo (scattering vector q ≈ 2.6 Å⁻¹) with a 10 µm beam at 7.32 keV at the pre-upgrade 8-ID-E; the upgraded beam and the narrower-band Si(311) setting at higher energy aim at faster atomic processes.

scienceCases.title: Nanoparticles at liquid interfaces, water clean-up and batteries
scienceCases.text: Many technologies depend on tiny particles or molecules collecting at the boundary between two liquids, or between a liquid and a solid: pulling toxic metals out of solution by solvent extraction, delivering drugs, or storing energy in flow-cell batteries. At such buried interfaces particles are held by energies of only a few times the thermal energy kT, and they lie beyond the reach of confocal light microscopy. The 2019 final design report names this the flagship case for small-angle speckle timing at 8-ID: it needs small, bright, coherent beams at higher energies to see how the particles arrange and move.

scienceCases.title: Fluctuations in quantum materials
scienceCases.text: In some materials the electrons spontaneously form ripples, called charge-density waves, or magnetic domains, and these patterns can flicker on their own. Wide-angle X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS), including Bragg XPCS, which times the speckle around a crystal reflection, can watch this flickering, which matters for future microelectronics and quantum computing. Talks at the July 2023 XPCS first-experiments workshop covered, for example, charge-density-wave fluctuations in TaS₂ and lattice dynamics in microelectronics. The sources present these as research directions, not yet as published 8-ID results.

scienceCases.title: Biomolecules and viruses in motion
scienceCases.text: X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS) can time how fast a virus or protein drifts through liquid, which gives its true size in solution and shows whether it is starting to clump, an early step in diseases linked to protein aggregation. Before the upgrade, 8-ID-I measured Cowpea mosaic virus diffusing with 19.2 µs time resolution and found an effective (hydrodynamic) radius 43–104% larger than the particle itself, depending on the buffer. The APS 2025–29 strategic plan targets the first steps of protein aggregation, down to two molecules pairing up, with the upgraded 8-ID. Radiation dose sets the limit, so moving the sample through the beam and using higher energies are essential.

scienceCases.title: Measuring nanoscale flow in driven soft matter
scienceCases.text: A new way to analyse speckle movies turns them into a flow meter for nanoparticles. Rather than averaging, it treats the two-time correlation maps of a system driven out of equilibrium with transport-coefficient methods from statistical physics, and was first checked against molecular-dynamics simulations. Applied to earlier creep and recovery measurements in the 8-ID-I rheometer on a suspension of charged silica nanoparticles (42% by volume), it resolved fractions moving at different speeds, such as several shear bands side by side, that a single time-averaged correlation curve would blur.

insertionDevices.type: planar hybrid permanent-magnet revolver undulator (two magnet arrays on a rotating strongback)

insertionDevices.notes: Arrays: APS21#9 (21 mm, N=112, Keff 1.38, E1 8.36 keV) and APS25#7 (25 mm, N=94, Keff 1.99, E1 4.58 keV). FDR design: two in-line revolvers U21/U25, 4.6 m total, max 2.0/2.2 kW through the 2 × 2 mm² mask.

source.canting: None – in-line tandem (dual in-line revolvers on one straight feeding a single beam), with phase shifter/corrector between the devices (FDR Table 3.13).
source.frontEnd: Standard APS-U High Heat Load Front End (based on 28-ID HHLFE): clearing magnet, LPPS, storage-ring valve, burn-through fixed mask BTFM1, FM2, collimator, GRID XBPM1, FM3, photon shutter PS2 with intensity monitor IM1, safety shutters SS1/SS2, wall collimator, front-end valve, exit mask (2 × 2 mm², XBPM2) at 25.4 m and exit collimator (5 × 5 mm²) at 26.1 m. Limits 21 kW and 590 kW/mrad². Windowless (differential pump) exit to preserve coherence.
source.sourceSizeAndDivergence: Electron beam at the ID (nominal, zero current; ops SR parameters): flat mode (κ = 0.1, 39.7/4.0 pm): σx = 14.5 µm, σx′ = 2.75 µrad, σy = 3.1 µm, σy′ = 1.29 µrad; round mode (κ = 1, 28.7 pm each): 12.3 µm, 2.34 µrad, 8.3 µm, 3.47 µrad. FDR Table 1.1 (with IBS at 200 mA): brightness mode 324 bunches, 42 pm: 14.7 / 2.8 / 3.2 / 1.3; timing mode 48 bunches, 32 pm: 12.9 / 2.5 / 8.8 / 3.7 (µm, µrad). Pre-upgrade APS: 280 / 11.6 / 10 / 3.4. Measured (Shi et al. 2025, grating interferometry at 3-ID-B, 11.3 keV, 50 mA): low coupling εx = 44 ± 3 pm, εy = 3.3 ± 2 pm (total photon source 16.1 × 4.9 µm rms); full coupling 28 ± 3 pm (H) / 31 ± 2 pm (V); 33 pm rad horizontal measured at 200 mA (April 2025). Single-electron photon terms for the 4.7 m effective undulator at 10 keV (Kim convention, derived here): σr ~2.7 µm, σr′ ~3.6 µrad → total photon source ~14.7 × 4.1 µm rms and ~4.6 × 3.9 µrad rms (flat mode); transverse coherence length λ L/(2 π Σ) at the CRL-1 position (52 m) ~70 µm (H) × ~250 µm (V) at 10 keV.

branches.name: Common optics (8-ID-A FOE, transport, 8-ID-D SOE)
branches.description: Undulators, front end, HHL mirrors, HDCM, (optional DMM), CRL-1 and diagnostics shared by both stations; all in-line on one beam axis.

branches.name: WA-XPCS mode (8-ID-E)
branches.description: Monochromatic beam focused by CRL-1 + KB to 0.3–3 µm on the six-circle diffractometer; detectors on the diffractometer arm (1.5–2 m) or LDDP (2.5–4 m).

branches.name: SA-XPCS mode (8-ID-I), beam-pass through 8-ID-E
branches.description: Pink or monochromatic beam passes 8-ID-E in a removable pipe; CRL-1 + CRL-2 focus to 3–10 µm at the 8-ID-I sample; 4–12 m telescoping flight tube. Pinhole USAXS combines the 8-ID-E sample position with the 8-ID-I detector (~22 m).

components.name: Upstream revolver undulator (APS21R25 #10: U21 / U25)
components.distanceNote: Approximate. Two ~2.35 m devices share the ~5 m straight with a phase shifter between; centre placed ~1.25 m upstream of the straight centre (the FDR distance origin). Not given explicitly in any source.
components.text: The upstream of the two undulators that make 8-ID's X-rays: a 2.35 m row of alternating permanent magnets that steers the 6 GeV electrons into a tight slalom, so they emit an intense, narrow X-ray beam. It is a revolver: two magnet rows with different periods (the repeat length of the magnet pattern, 21 mm and 25 mm) sit at 90° on one rotating support, and the device turns, with its gap open, to use whichever row gives the brighter beam at the chosen energy. At the 8.5 mm minimum gap the lowest fundamental energy is 4.54 keV with the 25 mm row and 8.34 keV with the 21 mm row; users work at gaps of 9.0 mm or more.

components.name: Phase shifter (corrector between the two revolvers)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: between the two devices at the straight centre (FDR Table 3.13 lists 'phase shifter/corrector' for the 08-ID dual in-line configuration).
components.text: A small magnet between the two undulators that delays the electrons by just the right amount, so the light from the second device arrives in step with the light from the first and the two add up, like two choirs singing the same note together. Steering correctors here keep the electron orbit straight. The design lists a phase shifter/corrector at this spot, but its type and exact position are not published.

components.name: Downstream revolver undulator (APS21R25 #4: U21 / U25)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (see upstream device).
components.text: The second, identical revolver undulator, directly behind the first. Set to the same magnet row and gap, and kept in step by the phase shifter, the pair acts like one 4.7 m light source and is brighter than either alone. Up to about 12 keV the beamline uses the fundamental of either row; above roughly 12–14 keV it switches to the 25 mm row's third harmonic, an overtone at three times the fundamental energy. The 21 mm row's fundamental tops out near 16 keV only with its gap opened so far that it gives little flux.

specs.harmonics used: fundamental to ~12 keV; U25 3rd harmonic above ~12–14 keV

components.name: High-heat-load front end (HHLFE, windowless)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: the front end occupies roughly 14–25 m inside the tunnel and through the ratchet wall; 20 m is a representative position for the GRID-XBPM/photon-shutter group. Component positions are not tabulated in the FDR.
components.text: The gatekeeper between the accelerator and the beamline, inside the concrete shielding. Water-cooled masks trim the beam, X-ray beam-position monitors check that it points exactly right, and shutters can stop it completely. This standard high-heat-load design of the upgraded APS is rated for 21 kW in total and 590 kW/mrad² at the centre of the beam. It has no exit window: a differentially pumped section keeps the vacuums apart instead, because even a thin window would spoil the beam's coherence.

specs.XBPMs: GRID XBPM1 + XBPM2 in exit mask

components.name: Front-end exit mask (2 × 2 mm²)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: A metal block with a 2 mm square opening, the last aperture of the front end. Seen from the source 25.4 m away, the opening spans only about 79 microradians (millionths of a radian), so just the bright central core of the undulator beam enters the beamline. A beam-position monitor (XBPM2) is built into the mask. The preliminary design had asked for an even narrower 40 × 40 µrad for this beamline.

components.name: Front-end exit collimator (5 × 5 mm²)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: A heavy tungsten block with a 5 mm square hole. It keeps bremsstrahlung (very-high-energy gamma rays produced when stored electrons strike leftover gas in the ring) from following the X-ray beam down the line. For the upgrade the opening was narrowed to 5 × 5 mm² so that beamlines whose optics shift the beam only slightly sideways can still keep the bremsstrahlung contained.

components.name: White-beam HHL slits (8ID-SL-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: Four jaws with tungsten edges that trim the raw white beam, which still contains every energy the undulators emit. The opening, up to 5 × 5 mm², sets how much beam reaches the optics, and how coherent it is: a narrower opening passes a weaker but more coherent beam. The whole assembly sits on a motorized table, so a set aperture can be scanned across the beam without moving the blades.

components.name: Mirror M1 (flat Si, horizontal deflection; 8ID-MR-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: A super-smooth flat silicon mirror, struck at a grazing 3.0 mrad (0.17°), that deflects the beam slightly sideways and takes most of the heat: about 370–425 W in the design cases. Its four stripes (bare silicon, chromium, rhodium and platinum) each reflect only up to a certain energy, so choosing a stripe filters out unwanted high-energy harmonics. Like all the beam-conditioning optics before the experiment stations, it bounces the beam sideways rather than up: the source is several times wider than it is tall, so a sideways wobble blurs the effective source far less. A side notch in the mirror cuts heat-induced bending about tenfold.

components.name: White/pink-beam diagnostics (8ID-BD-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: A beam camera and position monitor used to line up the undulator beam on the mirrors. The preliminary design pairs a white-beam position monitor with a fluorescent YAG (yttrium aluminium garnet) screen that works even with the undulator gap nearly open, a photocurrent monitor and a bypass aperture.

components.name: White-beam stop / mask (8ID-PM-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: A heavy block between the two mirrors that swallows the straight-through white beam and the bremsstrahlung travelling with it. Only the pink beam reflected by M1, which still spans a broad band of energies but has lost the highest ones, slips past it to the second mirror.

components.name: Mirror M2 (flat Si, horizontal deflection; 8ID-MR-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight). Listed in the FDR table as 'Horizontal, Focusing', whereas the FDR text describes both mirrors as flat with an optional bender on M2.
components.text: A second flat silicon mirror at the same 3.0 mrad grazing angle, with the same four stripes, that bounces the beam back so it runs parallel again, now about 16 mm to the side and out of line with the straight-through radiation. M1 has already absorbed most of the power, so M2 takes only 10–18 W. The design allows a mechanical or thermal bender to correct wavefront distortions from M1 and the monochromator; whether one is fitted is not documented.

components.name: Secondary collimator (8ID-SC-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: A lead-and-tungsten shielding block that confines stray scattered radiation to this first optics enclosure. The collimators here work with those in the front end, so the sideways-shifted beam passes while straight-through radiation is stopped.

components.name: Pink-beam mask / stop (8ID-PM-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: A mask that trims the pink beam (the mirror-filtered beam, still spanning a broad band of energies) to a clean outline and absorbs anything outside it. It has a built-in stop that can block the pink beam entirely.

components.name: Bremsstrahlung collimator (8ID-BC-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: A dense block that stops bremsstrahlung, the gamma rays born in the accelerator, so it can never reach the experiment stations. All of this primary bremsstrahlung is stopped in the first optics enclosure, which is why the second optics enclosure needs no collimators of its own.

components.name: Pink-beam diagnostics (8ID-BD-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: A monitor that checks the pink beam's position just before the monochromator crystals. Knowing where the beam lands on the crystals is the first step to keeping it steady downstream.

components.name: Pink-beam slits H+V (8ID-SL-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: Slits that trim the pink beam just before the crystal monochromator, so the crystals receive only the wanted part of the beam, and less heat.

components.name: Horizontal crystal monochromator (HDCM: LN₂-cooled Si(111)/Si(311); 8ID-MN-1, -MN-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: The monochromator picks out a single X-ray energy: two perfect silicon crystals, cooled with liquid nitrogen, reflect only the wavelength that matches their angle (Bragg's law). The Si(111) setting passes a band about 1.3 × 10⁻⁴ of the energy wide; Si(311) passes one about five times narrower, giving fewer photons but a longer coherence length along the beam, which wide-angle work needs. Like the mirrors, it deflects sideways rather than up, because speckle experiments need an exceptionally steady beam: the crystals must hold their pitch to within 40 nanoradians rms (root-mean-square). At 30 keV and 30 m, a sideways-deflecting pair tolerates about 100 nrad of vibration before it blurs the source by 10%, an upward-deflecting one only about 28 nrad. For pink-beam work the crystals move out of the way.

specs.vibration tolerance, 30 keV at 30 m: ~100 nrad (horizontal DCM) vs ~28 nrad (vertical) for 10% source broadening

components.name: Mode-switch mask (8ID-PM-3)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: A movable mask that is set differently for pink beam, which spans a broad band of energies, and for monochromatic beam, which carries a single energy. The monochromatic beam leaves the crystals about a centimetre to the side of the pink beam (10–15 mm, depending on the source document), so the opening has to follow whichever beam is in use.

components.name: Pink-beam shutter (8ID-SH-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: A heavy safety shutter that closes off the beam so people can work in the enclosures downstream while the first optics stay in operation. It is built to stop both pink and monochromatic beams.

components.name: Secondary collimator (8ID-SC-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: The last shielding block, at the downstream wall of the first optics enclosure. It keeps scattered radiation from following the beam pipe out onto the experiment floor.

components.name: Shielded transport (8ID-ST-1, -ST-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33: 36.0–47.0 m (start value given).
components.text: An 11 m lead-shielded vacuum pipe that carries the beam across the experiment floor, past the neighbouring 8-BM-B hutch, to the second optics enclosure. It has no windows: from the source to the experiment stations the beam stays in ultra-high vacuum, so that nothing degrades its coherent wavefront.

components.name: Pink-beam diagnostics (8ID-BD-3)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: A monitor at the entrance to the second optics enclosure that watches the beam arriving from the first. In the preliminary design it combines a diamond beam-position monitor, a fluorescent screen and a bypass aperture, to track how stable the beam is after its 11 m trip.

components.name: Pink-beam slits (8ID-SL-3)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: Slits, opening up to about 10 × 10 mm², that trim the beam ahead of the position planned for the multilayer monochromator. They limit stray beam and heat on the optics that follow.

components.name: Double multilayer monochromator (8ID-MN-3/4/5, status unconfirmed)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight). Not mentioned in the 2021 status talk nor in the 2026 directory (which lists only Si(111)/Si(311)); may not be installed. Drawn see-through because its installation is unconfirmed.
components.text: A planned in-between option: a double multilayer monochromator, two mirrors coated with alternating nanometre-thin layers that reflect a band of energies about 0.3–1% wide, far broader than the silicon crystals pass, giving many more photons when an experiment can tolerate it. It was designed for small-angle speckle work, which does not need the crystals' fine energy resolution, and must move fully out of the beam otherwise. Recent descriptions of the beamline do not mention it, so it may never have been installed; it is drawn see-through.

components.name: Mode-switch mask (8ID-PM-4)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: A second mode-switch mask, just downstream of the planned multilayer monochromator position. Like the first, it is set to match whichever beam, pink or monochromatic, is in use.

components.name: Pink-beam slits before CRL-1 (8ID-SL-4)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: These slits choose how much of the beam enters the first lenses, and so how many coherence patches, or transverse modes, are used. A smaller opening gives purer coherence and higher speckle contrast but fewer photons. For a single mode at 10 keV the preliminary design opens them to about 79 × 199 µm (width × height): taller than wide, because the source is smaller vertically and so the beam is coherent over a larger height. The design cases also use about 3.2 × 3.2 ≈ 10 modes, trading contrast for flux.

components.name: Transfocator CRL-1 (Be compound refractive lenses; 8ID-TR-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: The zoom lens shared by both experiment stations: a transfocator, 12 stacks of tiny curved beryllium lenses (compound refractive lenses) that slide in and out of the beam to focus more or less strongly. X-rays bend only very slightly in any material, so many lenses are stacked; the focal length is f = R/(2Nδ), where R is the lens radius, N the number of lenses and δ how far beryllium's refractive index falls below 1, about 3.4 × 10⁻⁶ at 10 keV and seven times less at 25 keV, which is why high energies need many more lenses. It works with the Kirkpatrick–Baez focusing mirrors for 8-ID-E or with CRL-2 for 8-ID-I. It is water-cooled so it can take pink beam, and slides sideways to follow the pink or monochromatic beam.

components.name: Beam-position diagnostics (8ID-BD-4)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: A beam-position monitor just after the lenses. It feeds back to keep the beam steady on the sample in 8-ID-E and works with pink or monochromatic beam.

components.name: Pink-beam shutter for 8-ID-E (8ID-SH-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: The safety shutter at the downstream end of the second optics enclosure that lets beam into the wide-angle station, 8-ID-E. Because the 8-ID-E optics take only monochromatic beam, it also serves as the pink-beam stop for 8-ID-E work.

components.name: 8-ID-E optics table (attenuators, experiment shutter, mono-beam slits 8ID-SL-5)
components.distanceNote: Slits SL-5 at 54.8 m per FDR Table 4.33; attenuators and experiment shutter share a motorized 6-DOF table (PDR TC1, 52.5–54.5 m in the 2017 layout) – positions approximate.
components.text: A heavy motorized table that can move and tilt along all six axes, carrying filters (attenuators) that dim the beam, a fast experiment shutter, and slits that clean up the beam before the final focusing mirrors. Everything on it works with monochromatic beam only. Only the slits have a tabulated position (54.8 m); the others are placed approximately.

components.name: KB focusing mirrors (bendable Kirkpatrick–Baez pair, 8ID-MR-3)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight). FDR text instead says VKB/HKB are 500/350 mm upstream of the sample (sample at 56.3–56.5 m), which is inconsistent with the table; PDR: optic-to-sample 0.4 m. Pair: VKB (deflects vertically) then HKB (horizontally), 2.5 mrad each.
components.text: Two curved mirrors in the Kirkpatrick–Baez (KB) arrangement, the first focusing up and down, the second side to side, squeeze the beam, together with the upstream lens stack CRL-1, to a spot as small as 0.3 µm, a few hundred times thinner than a hair. A tiny spot makes large speckles (speckle size ≈ wavelength × distance ÷ spot size), so atomic-scale speckle can be resolved at a practical detector distance. The platinum-coated mirrors meet the beam at 2.5 mrad and are bent to shape; their surfaces must match the ideal shape to within 1.0–1.5 nm rms (root-mean-square). Unlike lenses, mirrors focus every energy to the same point. The first mirror is the only optic on 8-ID that deflects the beam vertically.

specs.deflections: VKB vertical (upstream), HKB horizontal (downstream). Up/down direction of the VKB is not documented.

components.name: Be window (8ID-WN-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: A thin, X-ray-transparent beryllium window that separates the ultra-high vacuum of the optics from the sample area. It is chosen to preserve the beam's coherence.

components.name: Guard slits (8ID-SL-6)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: The last slits before the sample. They block the faint halo scattered by upstream optics, and the fringes diffracted by the edges of earlier slits, so that they do not swamp the sample's weak speckle.

components.name: Six-circle diffractometer (Huber design, with sample stack; 8ID-BI-1, -BI-3)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight). (FDR also quotes 56.4/56.5 m for the WA sample position elsewhere).
components.text: A large, very stiff six-circle diffractometer, a robotic sample holder that can tilt and turn a crystal to almost any angle, so scientists can aim at exactly the atomic reflection they want to watch flicker. Its split detector arm carries a close detector that swings upward and a rail that supports the long flight path to the far detector. Scattering upward has an advantage: the undulator light is polarized horizontally, so in the horizontal plane the scattered intensity falls as cos²(2θ) at large scattering angles 2θ, while in the vertical plane it does not. Its base slides aside to let the beam through to 8-ID-I.

components.name: 8-ID-E sample environments
components.distanceNote: At the diffractometer centre.
components.text: Interchangeable stages let materials be watched while hot, cold or stretched: a liquid-helium-cooled cryostage from 3.5 K (3.5 degrees above absolute zero) to 475 K, a vacuum heating dome up to 1,100 °C, and a tensile stage that pulls samples at anywhere from liquid-nitrogen temperature to 350 °C. The 2021 plan also listed a second heating and cooling stage (93–773 K).

specs.models: Lake Shore ST-500; Anton Paar DHS 1100; Linkam MFS

components.name: Removable beam-pass pipe (8ID-VP-2; for 8-ID-I and USAXS modes)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33: 57.3–61.0 m (start given). Drawn see-through, as the model shows 8-ID-E in WA mode.
components.text: A removable vacuum pipe. The two experiment stations take turns: when 8-ID-I is in use, the diffractometer slides aside and this 3.7 m pipe carries the beam straight through 8-ID-E. Its windows must survive pink beam, so they are water-cooled and purged with nitrogen. It is drawn see-through because this model shows 8-ID-E in wide-angle mode.

components.name: Vertical-arm WA detector (1.5–2 m, on the diffractometer arm)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: 1.5–2 m from the sample (MEDSI 2020); FDR lists the exit flight path 8ID-BI-2 at 58.0 m. Drawn at 1.6 m and 2θ = 30° upward on the vertical arm, i.e. at 57.7 m along the beam and 0.8 m above it (same illustrative setting as the LDDP).
components.text: A camera on the diffractometer's arm, 1.5–2 m from the sample, that swings upward to wide angles, up to 120° in the design, to catch the speckle made by atoms. Being close, it spreads each speckle over fewer pixels than the far detector does, but scattering upward avoids the polarization loss at large angles. A short flight pipe, anti-scatter slits and a remote filter box sit between it and the sample.

components.name: Long-distance detector positioner (LDDP: air-bearing base, removable flight path)
components.distanceNote: FDR lists detectors 8ID-DT-1 at 60.0 m (= ~3.7 m from sample); LDDP range 2.5–4 m from the sample. Drawn at R = 3.7 m and 2θ = 30° outboard, i.e. at 59.5 m along the beam and 1.85 m outboard (illustrative setting: the first sharp diffraction peak of a metallic glass, q ≈ 2.6 Å⁻¹, at ~10 keV).
components.text: The long-distance detector positioner: a granite block that floats on air cushions, so staff can glide the detector around the room and lock it 2.5–4 m from the sample at a horizontal scattering angle of 3–55°. Farther away, each speckle spreads over more pixels and is easier to resolve. Removable vacuum flight-path sections bridge the gap from the diffractometer, motorized stages fine-tune the position, and a laser tracker records exactly where the detector ended up.

components.name: Diagnostics for 8-ID-I (8ID-BD-5)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: A beam monitor that keeps the beam steered for the small-angle station, 8-ID-I. In the design it combines a diamond position monitor, a fluorescent screen and a bypass aperture, and its feedback corrects slow drifts of the monochromator and mirrors.

components.name: Pink-beam slits before CRL-2 (8ID-SL-7)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: Slits that select the coherent part of the beam entering the second set of lenses, CRL-2. As with the slits before CRL-1, the opening trades coherence against photon count; they open up to 10 × 10 mm² and can take pink beam.

components.name: Transfocator CRL-2 (8ID-TR-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: A second sliding stack of beryllium lenses, about five metres before the small-angle sample, with the same lens set as CRL-1. Working together, the two transfocators set the spot at the 8-ID-I sample between about 3 and 10 µm; simulations at 14.2 keV, with about ten coherent modes accepted, give 3.0 × 2.0 µm at the smallest and 11 × 8.5 µm at the largest. The whole unit travels ±300 mm along the beam to keep the focus on the sample across 8–25 keV.

components.name: Pink-beam shutter for 8-ID-I (8ID-SH-3)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: The safety shutter guarding the small-angle station, 8-ID-I. It can stop pink or monochromatic beam, so people can work in 8-ID-I while beam is delivered upstream.

components.name: Through-wall shielded pipe (8ID-ST-3, 8-ID-E/8-ID-I wall)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: A short shielded pipe that carries the beam through the wall between the two experiment stations. It is built to take pink beam, which 8-ID-I can use.

components.name: 8-ID-I guard slits #1 (8ID-SL-8)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: The first of three precision slits on 8-ID-I's upstream optical table that progressively clean the edges of the beam. Each stage trims the faint tails left by the one before. Between the slits and the sample the vacuum is held by differential pumping: separately pumped sections that step the pressure down without a window.

components.name: Fast shutter and attenuators (8-ID-I)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: on the upstream optical table (~64–66.5 m); not in the FDR table.
components.text: A shutter that opens and closes in under a millisecond, plus polished filters (attenuators) that dim the beam across 8–25 keV, so delicate samples get only the X-rays they need. They sit on the upstream optical table; the position shown is approximate.

components.name: 8-ID-I guard slits #2 (8ID-SL-9)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: The second of the three beam-cleaning slits on the upstream optical table. It trims the faint scatter left by the edges of the first.

components.name: 8-ID-I guard slits #3 (8ID-SL-10)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: The final beam-cleaning slit, just before the sample. Set just outside the beam, it catches scatter from the slits upstream without clipping the beam itself.

components.name: Be window (8ID-WN-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: A thin beryllium window where the vacuum beam path ends, just before the sample. Beryllium, a very light metal, lets X-rays through almost unhindered while holding the vacuum.

components.name: Sample table and rheometer (8-ID-I sample stage and environments incl. Rheo-XPCS; 8ID-BI-4, -BI-6)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight). The 2021 drawing places the sample table at ~66.1 m; treat ±1 m.
components.text: Where the small-angle sample sits. The sample table switches quickly between heated cells, including a holder that keeps up to nine samples at three temperatures between 0 and 160 °C, and a rheometer that shears a fluid in the gap between two cylinders (a Couette cell) while the X-rays watch its nanoscale structure move. The beam crosses the cell centre along the direction in which the flow speed changes, so the speckle records motion along the flow and along the cylinder axis.

components.name: 12 m SAXS flight tube (telescoping 4–12 m, rotatable 5°; 8ID-BI-5)
components.distanceNote: FDR: starts at 68.0 m, detector at 79.0 m. As-built (2025 abstract): sample-detector distance 4–12 m, horizontal rotation over 5° about the sample. Drawn fully extended (68.0–78.85 m); its pin sits at mid-length (73 m).
components.text: A vacuum tube up to 12 m long that lets the scattered X-rays travel far before they land, so each speckle grows big enough to be caught by single pixels: speckle size grows in proportion to distance. It telescopes from 4 to 12 m and swings up to 5° about the sample to reach larger angles, and its far end carries a motorized beam stop and a Kapton window. When stationary, the detector end must hold still to within 200 nm. In one published run at 12.4 keV with the detector at 11.6 m, it covered scattering vectors q from 0.04 to 0.51 nm⁻¹.

components.name: Fast photon-counting detectors (Rigaku Si 3-Mpixel PAD and Dectris EIGER2 X CdTe 4M; 8ID-DT-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR detector position at 79.0 m (12 m flight path end); moves with the telescoping tube. Drawn at the FDR position (11.5 m from the FDR sample position).
components.text: Photon-counting pixel detectors that register single X-ray photons in every pixel. The Rigaku silicon 3-megapixel detector records up to 56,000 frames a second continuously (19.2 µs time resolution) and close to a million a second in short bursts; at full speed it produces about 164 GB of raw data a second. The DECTRIS EIGER2 X CdTe 4M, whose cadmium-telluride sensor stops high-energy X-rays efficiently, runs at up to 4 kHz. The live pattern on this model's detector is a simulation, not data: the outer speckles twinkle faster because finer details change faster.

specs.fast PAD: Rigaku Si 3 MPix ('UHSS 3M'), 56 kHz continuous (2-bit readout per XSPA-500k characterization), burst up to ~1 MHz (13-frame bursts in the XSPA family)
specs.high-energy PAD: EIGER2 X CdTe 4M, up to 4 kHz (directory)

components.name: Beam stop (8ID-BS-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 (distance from source = centre of the ID straight).
components.text: The end of the line: a block at 80.6 m that safely absorbs whatever beam is left, pink or monochromatic. During measurements a small motorized stop inside the flight tube already catches the direct beam, so it never hits the detector.

enclosures.role: First optics enclosure (FOE), existing enclosure reused ('not changed')
enclosures.notes: PDR: spans 24–36 m. Contains FE exit table, WB slits, M1/M2, stops, collimators, HDCM, mode-switch mask, SH-1. Width approximate (~1.3 m outboard of beam to the ratchet-wall side ~0.6–1 m) from 2021 plan; abuts the storage-ring ratchet wall on its inboard side.

instruments.name: WA-XPCS instrument (six-circle diffractometer + LDDP)
instruments.text: The wide-angle station holds the sample on a heavy, ultra-steady six-circle diffractometer, which turns sample and detector about six axes, in a beam focused to 0.3–3 µm by a beryllium lens stack (CRL-1) and a pair of Kirkpatrick–Baez mirrors. Detectors sit either on the diffractometer's arm, 1.5–2 m away and swinging upward, or on the air-cushion long-distance positioner up to 4 m away at horizontal angles of 3–55°, where atomic-scale speckle spreads over more pixels. A laser tracker records the sample-to-detector geometry, and removable vacuum flight paths with anti-scatter slits cut air scatter. Three configurations are used: short-distance vertical scattering, long-distance horizontal scattering, and pinhole ultra-small-angle scattering with the detector in 8-ID-I. For 8-ID-I runs the diffractometer slides aside on its base.
detectors: Rigaku Si 3 MPix fast PAD (56 kHz, burst ~1 MHz)

instruments.name: SA-XPCS instrument (sample table + 4–12 m telescoping flight tube)
instruments.text: The small-angle station sends the scattered X-rays down a telescoping vacuum tube, 4–12 m long, to a fast photon-counting camera, so the speckles grow large enough to resolve. Two beryllium lens stacks, CRL-1 and CRL-2, set the spot at 3–10 µm, with pink or monochromatic beam. An upstream optical table carries three precision guard slits, a fast shutter, attenuators and beryllium windows, and the sample table swaps quickly between heated cells and a rheometer. The tube rotates up to 5° about the sample to reach larger angles, and a motorized beam stop and Kapton window close its far end.

instruments.name: Rheo-SAXS-XPCS (with Center for Nanoscale Materials)
instruments.text: A precision rheometer, offered with Argonne's Center for Nanoscale Materials, stirs, oscillates or holds a fluid in the gap between two cylinders while the X-rays look straight through it. The Anton Paar MCR 702e has two independent drives and a Couette cell; the beam crosses the cell centre along the direction in which the flow speed changes, so the speckle records motion along the flow and along the cylinder axis. Steady or oscillatory shear, creep and recovery tests run at the same time as speckle movies at 10 to 100,000 frames a second, so stress and strain can be compared directly with what the particles are doing.

instruments.name: Pinhole USAXS / US-XPCS configuration
instruments.text: This mode uses both stations as one long camera: the sample sits on the 8-ID-E diffractometer and the detector at the far end of the 8-ID-I flight tube, about 22 m away. The long distance resolves the very small angles scattered by the largest structures, up to micrometres in size, and their slow motion. The beam is opened to 15–45 µm, and the wide-angle detector in 8-ID-E can record at the same time.

geometryNotes:
The beamline uses a single in-line beam (no canting), entirely on the main experiment floor within sector 8 (no long-beamline building).

The enclosures follow this order: 8-ID-A FOE (existing, ~24.6–36.0 m) → ~11 m shielded transport (36–47 m) running past the 8-BM-B hutch → 8-ID-D SOE (~46.8–53.9 m, narrow, ~2 m wide) → 8-ID-E (53.9–63.7 m, wide and tallest, ~4.2 m roof) → 8-ID-I (63.7–81.6 m, a tapering wedge that extends beyond the normal hutch line into the aisle), with a new wedge-shaped control room alongside 8-ID-E/I on the outboard side; the 9-BM beamline runs on the inboard side.

All beam-transport optics upstream of the end stations deflect horizontally (the M1/M2 pair, the HDCM and the FDR's DMM); the only vertically deflecting optic is the VKB of the 8-ID-E KB pair (2.5 mrad, ~5 mrad beam deflection, direction undocumented).

The M1/M2 pair (28.0 and 30.6 m, 3 mrad) displaces the pink beam laterally by ~16 mm (PDR: toward inboard), and the HDCM adds a further fixed lateral offset (15 mm in the FDR, ~10 mm in the PDR and the 2021 talk; direction not documented). Downstream of 33.7 m the monochromatic beam axis is therefore ~25–31 mm sideways from the undulator axis, and the pink and monochromatic beams differ by ~10–15 mm laterally, hence the mode-switch masks and ±15 mm X travel on the transfocators and windows. There is no vertical offset upstream of the 8-ID-E KB: the beam height is constant through the FOE, transport, SOE and the 8-ID-I beam-pass.

The two stations operate one at a time: for 8-ID-I the WA instrument is moved aside (the diffractometer has X/Y base translations) and a removable vacuum pipe (57.3–61.0 m) is installed.

In 8-ID-E the horizontal-scattering LDDP arc (3–55°, up to 4 m) is drawn toward the control-room side; vertical scattering on the diffractometer arm is polarization-friendly because the undulator light is horizontally polarized.

In 8-ID-I the 12 m telescoping flight tube rides on a truss on two pedestals and rotates 5° about the sample, toward the inboard side in the 2021 drawing.

Distances in the FDR (2019) and the 2021 drawing differ by up to ~1 m in 8-ID-I (e.g. sample at 67.5 m vs ~66.1 m); hutch boundaries and widths here are read from the 2021 'Beamline Scope' drawing (scale bar 24–82 m) and are good to ±0.3 m. Each hutch has an overhead crane rail (elevation drawing). The beam height is not documented (the elevation suggests ~1.4 m; unverified).

The 3D model uses true distances and true hutch outlines (2021 plan, ±0.3 m), with hutch heights from the 2021 elevation. interactiveIdeas.title: Speckle TV: the twinkling fingerprint
interactiveIdeas.concept: A box of nanoparticles jiggles in water (adjust particle size, temperature, viscosity: water vs glycerol). A coherent beam illuminates them and a live 'detector' shows the far-field speckle |sum_j exp(i q.r_j)|² over a Gaussian beam footprint; it twinkles. Click a ring of pixels and watch g2(τ) build up and decay; the fit returns the diffusion coefficient and then the particle size via Stokes-Einstein.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Speckle is an interference fingerprint of particle positions; its fluctuation rate measures motion; bigger q (larger angle) decorrelates faster; viscosity and size set the time scale.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Siegert: g2 = 1 + β exp(−2 D q² τ) for Brownian motion (intensity decays at twice the field rate). D = kT/(6 π η R): R = 57 nm silica in water at 25 °C gives D ~4.3 × 10⁻¹² m²/s; at q = 0.05 nm⁻¹, 1/(Dq²) ~93 µs, g2 decay time ~46 µs (so µs detectors are needed); glycerol is ~1000× slower. q = 4 π sin(θ)/λ, λ[Å] = 12.398/E[keV]. Contrast β < 1 from partial coherence and pixel averaging. Use Poisson photon noise per pixel.

interactiveIdeas.title: Old APS vs APS-U: can you catch the motion?
interactiveIdeas.concept: Pick a sample relaxation time (1 ms down to 1 µs) and a source (APS 2019 vs APS-U). The simulated detector shows the real photon budget per frame (mostly 0s and a few 1s), the resulting noisy g2 curve and its signal-to-noise. Slide the frame rate up and watch the old source drown in shot noise while APS-U still resolves the decay.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why coherent flux, not total flux, matters; why XPCS time resolution improves with the square of brightness; why detectors need only 2-bit depth but huge frame rates.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: SNR(g2) ~ β * I_pix * sqrt(T * dt * N_pix) (valid for I_pix dt << 1); I_pix ~ Fc * (scattering cross-section) * solid angle per pixel; Fc = B λ²/4. Pre-upgrade benchmark ~2 × 10¹⁰ ph/s coherent (7.4 keV, 8-ID-I, 2016) vs design ~10¹³ ph/s (Si(111), ~10 keV, 1 mode). At fixed SNR, dt_min scales as Fc⁻². Do not imply single-pixel counts > a few per frame at µs frames.

interactiveIdeas.title: Zoom optics and speckle matching
interactiveIdeas.concept: Drag lens cartridges (Be CRLs, R = 100–1000 µm) into CRL-1 and CRL-2 or flatten/bend the KB, choose an energy 8–25 keV, and see the spot at the sample (0.3–3 µm in 8-ID-E, 3–10 µm in 8-ID-I). A second panel shows the speckle size on the detector versus the 75 µm pixel at a chosen distance (1.5–12 m); contrast drops when speckles become smaller than pixels.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Small beams make big speckles; long flight tubes make speckles bigger; high energies need more lenses and longer distances; trade-off between spot size, coherent modes accepted and flux.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Thin-lens CRL: f = R/(2 N δ), δ_Be ~3.4 × 10⁻⁶ at 10 keV scaling ~1/E² (~5.4 × 10⁻⁷ at 25 keV) → f ~1.5 m (10 keV) vs ~9 m (25 keV) for N = 10, R = 100 µm. Speckle size s = λ R / a: 10 keV, a = 3 µm, R = 12 m → ~0.5 mm; a = 10 µm → ~150 µm; 25 keV, a = 10 µm, 12 m → ~60 µm (< pixel, contrast loss). WA: 10 keV, a = 0.3 µm, 1.5 m → ~0.6 mm. KB achromatic, CRL chromatic. Keep the far-field condition R > a²/λ.

interactiveIdeas.title: Two-time map: watch a gel or glass age
interactiveIdeas.concept: An animated speckle movie of an aging colloidal gel (or a metallic glass at 668 K) feeds a growing two-time correlation map C(t1,t2). Sliders control aging exponent and add intermittent 'avalanches'. Visitors see the diagonal ribbon widen as the sample slows and squares appear at avalanche events.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Non-equilibrium materials change their own dynamics with time; a single averaged g2 hides this; two-time maps reveal aging and intermittency (as in the 83-hour metallic-glass run).
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: C(t1,t2) = <I(t1)I(t2)>/(<I(t1)><I(t2)>) over pixels at fixed q; width of the diagonal ~ τ(t_age) ~ t_age^µ; KWW f = exp[-(t/τ)^β_KWW] with compressed β_KWW ~1.2–2 typical of stress-driven glass dynamics; 'stationary' regimes show constant ribbon width.

interactiveIdeas.title: Shear it! Rheo-XPCS and speckle beats
interactiveIdeas.concept: A Couette cell (two cylinders) with a stress/shear-rate dial. The visitor shears a dense suspension: rheology plots viscosity and stress, while g2 along the flow direction decays faster and shows beats when a jammed network coexists with mobile particles; along the vorticity direction it does not.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: How macroscopic 'feel' (thickening, yielding, memory) maps onto nanoscale motion; why direction matters in sheared samples; what heterodyne beats mean.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Beam along the velocity-gradient direction, q in the flow-vorticity plane. Uniform shear in the illuminated gap gives an extra flow-direction decorrelation ~sinc²(q_par * γ̇ * w * τ / 2) (w = path length through sheared region); two populations with relative velocity v give cos(q.v τ) oscillations in g2; vorticity-direction g2 reflects non-affine (diffusive) motion only.

interactiveIdeas.title: Why 8-ID-E has a camera that looks up
interactiveIdeas.concept: Show horizontally polarized undulator light (field vectors drawn) scattering from a sample; rotate a detector around the sample in the horizontal plane and in the vertical plane and plot intensity vs 2θ.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Undulator X-rays are polarized; scattering in the polarization plane vanishes near 90°; that is why 8-ID-E has both a horizontal long arm (finer speckle, smaller angles) and a vertical arm (large angles).
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Thomson factor for horizontal polarization: horizontal-plane scattering ~cos²(2θ), vertical-plane ~1. 2θ = 55° (LDDP max) → cos²(55°) = 0.33 relative intensity; zero at 90°; vertical arm reaches 120° (PDR). q at 2θ = 55°: 4.7 Å⁻¹ (10 keV), 11.7 Å⁻¹ (25 keV).

interactiveIdeas.title: Coherence detective: transverse and longitudinal
interactiveIdeas.concept: Two sliders: slit opening (number of coherent modes accepted) and monochromator choice (pink ~0.5%, Si(111), Si(311)). A sample-thickness slider and a scattering angle slider; the speckle contrast meter falls when the path-length difference exceeds the longitudinal coherence length or the slit exceeds the transverse coherence length.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Coherence has two parts; small angles tolerate broad bandwidth (pink beam gives ~100× more photons), wide angles need narrow bandwidth.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Longitudinal coherence ξL ~ λ²/Δλ: at 10 keV ~0.95 µm (Si(111)), ~4.6 µm (Si(311)), ~25 nm (0.5% pink). Path-length difference in transmission PLD ~ 2 t sin²(θ) + w sin(2θ) (t = thickness, w = beam width in the scattering plane); contrast survives while PLD is <~ ξL. Note the convention: ξL = λ²/Δλ here (PDR); some texts use λ²/(2 Δλ), which is half as large. Transverse coherence ~λ L/(2 π Σ): at 52 m, 10 keV ~70 µm (H) × ~250 µm (V) for APS-U.

funFacts: 8-ID was the first APS Upgrade feature beamline to welcome users, in November 2024 (a group from the University of Akron).
X-ray speckle was first observed in 1991 (Sutton, Mochrie and co-workers, Nature); the technique's pioneers Grübel, Mochrie and Sutton received the APS Compton Award in 2009.

When photon counts set the limit, a 100× gain in coherent flux can give 10,000× shorter XPCS frames at the same quality, holding acquisition time, speckle contrast and pixel count fixed. Detector speed and dose can limit the gain.
Each undulator is a 'revolver': two magnet rows with different periods (21 and 25 mm) sit at 90° on one rotating strongback, and the device spins to load the one that gives the brightest beam.
One Rigaku 3-Mpixel detector at 56,000 frames per second produces ~164 GB/s of raw data; the beamline expects up to ~20 PB per year, ~200× more than before the upgrade.
A wide-angle XPCS run on a metallic glass at 8-ID-E lasted 83 hours (300,000 s) – one speckle snapshot every 2.5 s – revealing atoms that rearrange in bursts.
The monochromator was specified to vibrate less than 40 nanoradians – the angle a human hair (~80 µm) subtends from 2 km away.

The old 8-ID-E and 8-ID-I stations, then two of the longest and tallest enclosures at the APS, hosted more than 3,000 experiments over 25 years. In 2022 a team of six emptied both of them in under 14 days to make way for the upgrade (reported 3 October 2022).
The small-angle hutch 8-ID-I is so long (with a 12 m flight tube and a 22 m USAXS mode) that it needed formal approval to extend beyond the standard experiment-floor aisle.
Before the upgrade, 8-ID-I already timed a virus (Cowpea mosaic virus) diffusing in solution with 19 µs resolution, and XPCS on a free-hanging robotic pendant drop with 3.7 µs resolution.

openQuestions: Double multilayer monochromator (FDR 8ID-MN-3/4/5 at 49 m): not mentioned in the 2021 status talk or the 2026 directory (only Si(111)/Si(311)); it may have been descoped or deferred.
Exact as-built component positions: FDR 2019 Table 4.33 and the 2021 drawing differ by up to ~1 m in 8-ID-I (e.g. sample at 67.5 m vs ~66.1 m). No as-built component table is public.
HDCM lateral offset: 15 mm (FDR Fig. 4.23) vs ~10 mm (PDR, 2021 talk). Its direction (inboard or outboard) is not documented.

KB position: FDR table puts the KB at 55.3 m while its text puts the VKB/HKB 500/350 mm upstream of a sample at 56.3–56.5 m, which would place them downstream of the Be window at 55.7 m. The table order is used here.
M2 is described as flat with an optional bender in the FDR text but labelled 'Focusing' in the FDR component table. The as-built bender status is unknown.
8-ID-I flight path: 4–12 m (2025 abstract) vs 2–12 m (2021 requirement).

Energy range: 8–25 keV (FDR), 4.8–25 keV (2021 WA table), 6–25 or 7–25 keV (2026 directory). The practical low-energy limit with the U25 fundamental (E1 ≥ 4.5 keV at the 8.5 mm minimum gap) and the HDCM is not documented.

Detector identities: the Rigaku 'Si 3 MPix' model name is not public (the computing strategy calls it 'UHSS 3M'). The '4 kHz' quoted for the Eiger CdTe 4M matches the APS planning table (4.0 MB frames at 4 kHz, i.e. 1 byte/pixel). This suggests a reduced-bit-depth mode, but that is not confirmed by DECTRIS specifications.

No peer-reviewed commissioning paper with measured APS-U coherent flux, speckle contrast or stability at 8-ID was found (as of 8 October 2026). The quoted coherent-flux numbers are design or directory values.
Start of operations: the 8-ID page says general-user operations began in October 2024, while the news reports first users in early November 2024.
Inboard/outboard orientation (control room, LDDP arc and flight-tube rotation side) is inferred from the 2021 plan drawing, not stated explicitly.
The upstream and downstream revolver centre positions in the straight, and the phase-shifter details, are approximate.

Coherent flux in the 2021 WA-XPCS table (1–2 × 10¹² ph/s, 1 mode, Si(111), 8–25 keV) is ~10× below the FDR/PDR design values (1.6–1.7 × 10¹³ at 8.8–10 keV). The source of the difference is undocumented, and no measured as-built value is public.
Up/down direction of the 8-ID-E VKB deflection, and the resulting WA sample height relative to the beam axis, are not documented.
